newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ not worried about NZ Post's prospects - minister.
newsitem.headline: NZ not worried about NZ Post's prospects - minister.

text.p: The New Zealand government said on Tuesday it was not concerned about the ability of monopoly domestic mail service New Zealand Post to repay its debts and to continue its business after planned market liberalisations launched earlier in the day.
At a news conference, Communications Minister Maurice Williamson repeated that privatisation was not on the current government's agenda.
Separately, NZ Post issued a statement saying it welcomed the announced deregulation and expected the strong growth it had seen in all areas of its business recently to continue.
Williamson said the government expected the new regime to be in place by April 1, 1998, at the latest.

Detailing the plan, which will allow competition across the domestic light letter market for the first time, he said that current five- or six-day delivery frequency patterns would be guaranteed nationwide for NZ Post.

This protection of service agreements, and a three-year cap on letter rates for non-urgent post of NZ$0.45 (compared to a current letter rate of 40 cents), would form part of a so-called 'Kiwi Share' contract intended to protect consumer interests.
In its statement, state-owned NZ Post quoted its chief executive Elmar Toime as saying the company was ready to operate in a fully-competitive market.
It had been experiencing strong growth in all areas of its business over recent years "and expects this to continue".
Williamson echoed the sentiment at a news conference, saying, "New Zealand Post has told us they can continue to be a very profitable and viable company."
"This will get us away from claims NZ Post uses revenue from its monopoly to cross-subsidse other areas of its business, such as couriers," he added.
The Postal Services Bill is due for its second reading next week.

NZ Post was corporatised in 1987 and has been competing for several years with courier companies for the carriage of a range of heavier and time-sensitive items where price regulations have already been removed.
